newsitem.title: USA: NAACP says affirmative action still needed.
newsitem.headline: NAACP says affirmative action still needed.

text.p: Congressional attempts to kill affirmative action must be killed themselves because blacks and other minorities are still victims of massive discrimination, government and NAACP officials said Wednesday.

Speaking on a panel that focused on affirmative action, leaders of the NAACP and government agencies urged a large audience of African Americans to write to their congressional representatives and demand they block passage of the McConnell-Canady bill, named for the politicians who sponsored it.
"There's a perception that if (this bill) gets to the floor, it will pass," said Harold McDougall, director of the NAACP's Washington bureau. "The representatives really need to hear from us."

The bill, sponsored by Republicans Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky and Representative Charles Canady of Florida, would eliminate federal affirmative action programmes. There are 53 other members of Congress who signed on as co-sponsors.
Gregory Stewart, general counsel at the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, said race -- not age or gender -- continued to be the single largest factor in discrimination in the workplace.
"The EEOC is refocusing on race. Race charges continue to be the largest single charge filed with the EEOC," he said.
Stewart said there has been a "troubling increase" during the past few years in the number of cases filed that allege discrimination based on race.

He said there also has been a large increase in the number of cases filed in which black employees complained of harassment, including having nooses hung in their lockers or pictures of monkeys placed on their personal belongings.
He said there are a number of cases filed every year that allege reverse discrimination -- discriminatory practices against whites -- but cases filed by blacks far outnumber those.
"It's clear to us that affirmative action is still needed," he said.

Gale Barron Black, executive assistant at the U.S. Labour Department, said the black unemployment rate remains twice as high as the unemployment rate among whites. "It's mind-boggling that what we do -- we do affirmative action -- is under attack," she said.
